title: The Spell and the Registrar: Jaffna, a Village on the Khorat Plateau, and the Words That Do Things
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Jaffna, the lawyer's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the National Academy of Sciences biographical memoir gives 16 January 1929 and names Jaffna, Northern Province. Town-centre coordinates: no birth address or hospital is recorded.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of January a son is born in Jaffna, in the Tamil north of British Ceylon, one of nine children in an English-speaking Anglican household. His father is a lawyer out of a family that owns coconut plantations; his mother comes down from a line of feudal district chiefs. The house runs three registers at once, Tamil in the street, English at the table, the Book of Common Prayer on Sunday. They name him Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah. The memoir that records the birth gives the town and the date. It does not give an address, and it does not give an hour.
suggested_refs: Jaffna town, Northern Province, birthplace and the site of the university that will honor him in 1980
sources: Emiko Ohnuki-Tierney, 'Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah 1929-2014,' Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences (2015)

stops.name: S. Thomas' College, Mount Lavinia: the dormitory of four communities
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed year: the memoir says he entered at age eleven, which places entry around 1940. Month and day defaulted. Coordinates are the historic Mount Lavinia campus on Hotel Road, confirmed to within about 130 metres.
stops.campa: At eleven he is sent to S. Thomas' College at Mount Lavinia, down the coast road from Colombo, an Anglican boarding school where Tamil, Sinhalese, Burgher and Muslim boys sleep in the same dormitories and sit the same examinations. The categories that divide the island are suspended inside the walled compound for the length of a term, which is a thing he learns before he learns any anthropology. The family keeps a house in Colombo, and the dinner table there is where he learns to argue. He has two years at Mount Lavinia before the war reaches the coast.
suggested_refs: S. Thomas' College, Mount Lavinia, Hotel Road, Dehiwala-Mount Lavinia

stops.name: Gurutalawa, the school sent up into the hills
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the memoir dates the move to after the fall of Singapore, February 1942, without giving a month. Coordinates are approximate, supplied at about 6.35N 80.92E by the verification pass and not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Singapore falls in February and the war reaches the island's coasts. The army requisitions the Mount Lavinia campus for a military hospital, and the school sends its boys inland and upward, to its hill-country branch at Gurutalawa in Uva Province, where the tea runs to the ridgelines and there is nothing to do after lessons but walk. He is thirteen. Seventy years later a colleague asks him about the hill years, and what he answers is the whole of what the record keeps of them.
stops.quote_source: Tambiah on the Gurutalawa years, reported in the NAS Biographical Memoir (2015)
suggested_refs: S. Thomas' College, Gurutalawa, Uva Province, the wartime branch campus

stops.name: College House, Colombo: the University of Ceylon
stops.date_confidence: the degree is attested to 1951; the entry year is a reconstruction from a normal four-year course. Coordinates are the Colombo campus at College House, Cumaratunga Munidasa Mawatha, not the Colombo Fort city centre that some listings give.
stops.campa: He reads for his degree at the University of Ceylon, in the colonial buildings on Thurstan Road, while the university is already packing itself for the move up-country to Peradeniya. He takes the degree in 1951. Nothing in the record suggests that anthropology is yet the plan; the monks and the spirit doctors are ten years off. What he is being trained in is sociology of the survey kind, questionnaires, sample villages, tables of landholding and income, the discipline a newly self-governing country wants because it produces numbers.
suggested_refs: College House, University of Ceylon, Colombo, the pre-Peradeniya campus

segments.name: Ithaca, and the Return of a Quantitative Man

stops.name: Cornell University, Ithaca: the hill above the lake
stops.date_confidence: arrival reconstructed from the attested 1954 doctorate; month defaulted to the academic year. Coordinates are the Cornell campus per Nominatim, correcting a widely copied pin two kilometres southwest on Ithaca's West Hill.
stops.campa: He crosses to upstate New York, to a university on a hill above a long cold lake, and enters a department that believes rural life can be counted. Ithaca in winter is a distance from Jaffna by every measure available. He works in rural sociology of the quantitative kind, the kind that produces coefficients and regression tables, and the training holds in him for a full decade. For now the instrument is the questionnaire, the unit of study is the household, and the village on the Khorat plateau that will break all of it open is ten years and half a world away.
suggested_refs: Cornell University, Ithaca, New York

stops.name: Ithaca, the doctorate conferred
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: the memoir states a Cornell PhD in 1954 and reproduces a photograph captioned to that year. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The doctorate is conferred in 1954. He goes home a rural sociologist with a quantitative approach, which is exactly what the island's planners want out of him. The second half of his life will be spent showing that the approach cannot describe what people do when they speak. A photograph survives from that year, captioned only as Stanley Tambiah, graduate student, Cornell University: a young man in a jacket, three years out of Ceylon. Nobody wrote down who took it.
suggested_refs: The 1954 Cornell graduate-student photograph reproduced in the NAS memoir

stops.name: Peradeniya, teaching in the Mahaweli valley
stops.date_confidence: CONTESTED and not resolved here: the NAS memoir dates the University of Ceylon post 1951-1960, Wikipedia dates it 1955-1960. The two reconcile if 1951 is the appointment and 1955 the return to residence after Cornell, but no source consulted says so. Both agree the post ends in 1960.
stops.campa: He teaches at the University of Ceylon on the new campus laid out below Kandy in the valley of the Mahaweli, among the first generation of the island's academic sociologists. With N. K. Sarkar he works up village survey material: land, income, household, the categories his Cornell training supplies. Whether the post begins in 1951 and is held from Ithaca on leave, or begins in 1955 when he comes home with the doctorate, the two sources that record it do not agree. They agree that it ends in 1960.
suggested_refs: University of Ceylon, Peradeniya campus, near Kandy
N. K. Sarkar and S. J. Tambiah, village survey work of the later 1950s

segments.name: Thailand: The Village and the Spirits

stops.name: Bangkok, the UNESCO posting
stops.date_confidence: the employment is attested, the city is not. The memoir says only that he worked as a technical assistance expert in Thailand for UNESCO until 1963; no source consulted names Bangkok, and this pin is a reconstruction from where such a posting would ordinarily sit. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: He leaves university teaching to work in Thailand as a technical assistance expert for UNESCO. The posting runs to 1963, and it is what puts him in the country. The one source that records it names the country and not the city; the pin sits at Bangkok because a UNESCO posting in Thailand in 1960 would ordinarily sit at Bangkok, and for no better reason than that. What does a technical assistance expert actually do, week by week, in Thailand in 1960? Nothing consulted this pass answers that.
suggested_refs: UNESCO technical assistance programme in Thailand, 1960-1963

stops.name: Baan Phraan Muan, Udon Thani: the village that keeps two religions
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the fieldwork is conventionally dated to the early 1960s from the 1970 monograph, and no source consulted gives exact years. The pin is the provincial town of Udon Thani, not the village itself, whose coordinates were not verified this pass.
stops.campa: Northeast, on the Khorat plateau near Udon Thani, he settles into a village called Baan Phraan Muan and does the thing his Cornell training never asked of him: he stays, and he watches. The village keeps a Buddhist temple and a full working population of spirits at the same time, without embarrassment, and monks and spirit doctors divide the labour between them along lines nobody in the village finds contradictory. He is thirty-two. The survey forms stay in the bag.
suggested_refs: Baan Phraan Muan, Udon Thani province, fieldwork site of 'Buddhism and the Spirit Cults in North-East Thailand'
sources: Tambiah, 'Buddhism and the Spirit Cults in North-East Thailand' (Cambridge UP, 1970)

stops.name: Baan Phraan Muan, the words said over the water
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed, and dated only to order the segment. The ethnographic content is drawn from the 1970 monograph and the 1968 article rather than from any dated field note; the fieldwork years themselves are not established.
stops.campa: What he records above all is speech. Monks chant Pali the villagers do not follow as language and hold to be effective as sound; blessings are said over water and the water is changed by them; a rite addresses a person's fled spirit-essence directly and calls it back into the body. An older anthropology would file the whole of it as mistaken physics, primitive men reasoning badly about causes. Sitting in the compound listening, he can hear that they are not reasoning badly about causes. They are doing something else with words.
suggested_refs: The chants, blessings and spirit-calling rites recorded at Baan Phraan Muan, published 1970
sources: Tambiah, 'Buddhism and the Spirit Cults in North-East Thailand' (1970)
Tambiah, 'The Magical Power of Words,' Man n.s. 3(2): 175-208 (1968)

segments.name: Cambridge, and the Words That Do Things

stops.name: Free School Lane, Cambridge: Leach opens the door
stops.date_confidence: CONTESTED: Wikipedia dates the Cambridge appointment to 1963, the NAS memoir to 1964. Not resolved here. Month defaulted. Coordinates are the Department of Social Anthropology site on Free School Lane, inherited from the Cambridge pin used across the corpus.
stops.campa: Edmund Leach brings him to Cambridge, to the Department of Social Anthropology on Free School Lane, and the ten years that follow are the ones his memorialist will call perhaps the best of his career. He arrives with a village in his notebooks and the discipline's whole quarrel over magic waiting for him in the reading room: Tylor, Frazer, Malinowski, Evans-Pritchard, the long argument about whether the savage thinks. Wikipedia dates the arrival to 1963. The Academy memoir dates it to 1964.
suggested_refs: Department of Social Anthropology, Free School Lane, Cambridge

stops.name: Bedford Square, London: the Curl Bequest Prize
stops.date_confidence: the prize and its year are attested by the memoir. The location is a reconstruction: no source consulted establishes the Royal Anthropological Institute's 1964 premises, and the Curl is an essay prize with no attested ceremony, so this stop is a place-holder for an award rather than a scene. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The Royal Anthropological Institute awards him the Curl Bequest Prize, which is given for an essay. There is no recorded ceremony and no date inside the year; an essay prize is a letter and a cheque. The pin sits at Bedford Square because that is where the Institute is generally taken to have been housed in 1964, and no source consulted actually says so. It is the first recognition the British discipline gives him. The same Institute gives him its Huxley Medal thirty-three years later.
suggested_refs: Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, Curl Bequest Prize 1964

stops.name: The London School of Economics, the Malinowski Memorial Lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested: the memoir records the Malinowski Memorial Lecture at the LSE and the article's citation as Man, new series, 3(2): 175-208 (1968). Month not given, defaulted.
stops.campa: He gives the Malinowski Memorial Lecture at the London School of Economics and prints it as The Magical Power of Words, in Man, volume three, pages 175 to 208. J. L. Austin, eight years dead, had shown that certain utterances describe nothing and cannot be true or false: they name ships, they marry people, they lay bets, and they either take or misfire. Tambiah puts the spell and the blessing into that box. Austin, who had worked the whole thing out at Oxford, never once examined either of them.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'The Magical Power of Words,' Man n.s. 3(2): 175-208 (1968)
J. L. Austin, 'How to Do Things with Words' (Clarendon, 1962)
sources: Standard citation, Man, new series, vol. 3, no. 2 (1968)

stops.name: Cambridge, the village becomes a book
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1970. The end of the Cambridge post is CONTESTED and not resolved: Wikipedia closes it in 1972 and describes nine years, the NAS memoir closes it in 1973 and calls the span ten years. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Buddhism and the Spirit Cults in North-East Thailand comes out of the Cambridge years and out of Baan Phraan Muan: an ethnography of a village that runs two religious systems at once and finds them compatible. It is the book that fixes his name in Southeast Asian studies, and he is forty-one when it appears. The post ends after a decade, or after nine years, according to which source is counting; Wikipedia closes it in 1972 and the Academy memoir in 1973.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Buddhism and the Spirit Cults in North-East Thailand' (Cambridge UP, 1970)

stops.name: The University of Chicago, three years on the South Side
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both the memoir and Wikipedia; month defaulted to the academic year. Coordinates are the Hyde Park campus, correcting a Loop city-centre pin ten kilometres north that circulates in some listings.
stops.campa: He crosses back over the Atlantic for a professorship at the University of Chicago, in Hyde Park, and stays three years. What comes out of them is a book about kingship, about what a king's words do, which is the village problem at the scale of a state. Otherwise the record is thin. No lecture series is listed, no quarrel is preserved, no anecdote has been thought worth keeping by anyone who knew him there. The Academy memoir disposes of the whole Chicago passage in six words.
suggested_refs: University of Chicago, Department of Anthropology, Hyde Park

stops.name: Chicago, World Conqueror and World Renouncer
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1976, Cambridge University Press. The subtitle is given here as the memoir's bibliography prints it, A Study of Religion and Polity in Thailand, correcting the widely copied misquotation A Study of Buddhism and Polity. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: World Conqueror and World Renouncer: A Study of Religion and Polity in Thailand against a Historical Background, Cambridge University Press. Two figures stand at either end of Buddhist political thought, the monarch who rules the world and the monk who walks out of it, and the book is about how a Thai state holds both and requires both. The mandala model it is famous for, the galactic polity of concentric courts each replicating the centre, gets its name a year later in a paper for the New York Academy of Sciences.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'World Conqueror and World Renouncer' (Cambridge UP, 1976)
Tambiah, 'The galactic polity: the structure of traditional kingdoms in Southeast Asia,' Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 293: 69-97 (1977)

segments.name: The Rabb Chair, and a Performative Approach to Ritual

stops.name: Harvard University, the chair he holds until he dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1976 by the memoir, which also confirms the Esther and Sidney Rabb chair. Month defaulted. Coordinates are the Harvard Yard pin used across the corpus, correcting a chronology value six hundred metres east of the campus.
stops.campa: He is called to Harvard as Esther and Sidney Rabb Professor of Anthropology, a chair he will hold until he is made emeritus and hold in that form until he dies. He is forty-seven. In twenty-five years he has taught in Ceylon, Thailand, England and America, and the island he was born on has changed its name and its terms inside his lifetime. Cambridge, Massachusetts is where the rest of it happens: the remaining books, the honours, the quarrel with his own country. He takes no other post after this one.
suggested_refs: Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts
The Esther and Sidney Rabb Professorship of Anthropology

stops.name: Burlington House, London: the Radcliffe-Brown Lecture
stops.date_confidence: lecture and year attested; month not recorded. Citation confirmed as Proceedings of the British Academy vol. LXV, pp. 113-169. The quotation below is reproduced verbatim across the ritual-studies literature but the original lecture text could not be fetched this pass, so it is carried as [R].
stops.campa: At Burlington House he gives the British Academy's Radcliffe-Brown Lecture in Social Anthropology, titled A Performative Approach to Ritual, and prints it in the Proceedings, volume sixty-five, pages 113 to 169. Eleven years on from the Malinowski lecture, the borrowing from Austin has become a general theory: a rite is not defective science but a species of act, governed by conditions of felicity rather than by truth, and it fails the way a marriage fails when the man at the desk turns out not to be a registrar.
stops.quote: Ritual is a culturally constructed system of symbolic communication. It is constituted of patterned and ordered sequences of words and acts, often expressed in multiple media, whose content and arrangement are characterized in varying degree by formality (conventionality), stereotypy (rigidity), condensation (fusion), and redundancy (repetition).
stops.quote_source: Stanley J. Tambiah, 'A Performative Approach to Ritual,' Radcliffe-Brown Lecture in Social Anthropology, Proceedings of the British Academy 65 (1979)
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'A Performative Approach to Ritual,' Proceedings of the British Academy LXV (1979), pp. 113-169, OUP offprint, Open Library OL22102141M
sources: Ritual-studies secondary literature, for the quoted definition

stops.name: The University of Jaffna, a doctorate from the north
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1980 by the memoir. Whether he travelled to Jaffna to receive it is not established by any source consulted; the stop marks the conferral, not a confirmed visit. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The University of Jaffna, a few miles from the house where he was born, makes him a Doctor of Letters. The town is not what it was and is about to become something worse: inside three years the north will be a war zone and the university will spend two decades operating under conditions no institution is built for. Whether he went up to receive it, no source consulted says. It is the first honorary degree he is given, and it comes out of the Tamil north. Chicago and Peradeniya follow eleven years later.
suggested_refs: University of Jaffna, Northern Province, Sri Lanka

stops.name: Oxford, the Radhakrishnan Memorial Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1982 by the memoir; no month, no titles recorded. Coordinates are the Oxford pin inherited from j_l_austin.journey.json, byte-identical.
stops.campa: He delivers the Radhakrishnan Memorial Lectures at Oxford, the university where J. L. Austin had worked out the performative and the felicity condition across the Saturday mornings of the early fifties and never once applied any of it outside English. Tambiah has by now applied it to Thai chants, to Sinhala blessings and to the whole ethnographic record of magic, and he brings it back into an English hall to lecture on Indian material. The memoir gives the year and the name of the series. It does not record what the lectures were called.
suggested_refs: Radhakrishnan Memorial Lectures, University of Oxford, 1982

stops.name: Cambridge, the Kingsley Martin Memorial Lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1982 by the memoir, which gives the year only. The month here is arbitrary and set solely to order this stop against the Oxford lectures of the same year; no sequence between the two is established.
stops.campa: He returns to Cambridge, to the university that gave him his best decade, for the Kingsley Martin Memorial Lecture. The memoir that lists it gives the year and nothing else: no title, no month, no room, no report of who came. The series is named for the long editor of the New Statesman, which makes it an occasion for talking politics rather than method. It is 1982, a year before the burning in Colombo, and the politics of his own island is already turning into the subject that will take the rest of his working life. Whether he spoke about Sri Lanka in that hall, there is no way from here to know.
suggested_refs: Kingsley Martin Memorial Lecture, University of Cambridge, 1982

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts: the news out of Colombo
stops.date_confidence: the pogrom is attested to July 1983 and is widely documented. Tambiah's own whereabouts that month are NOT established by any source consulted, so the stop sits at his Harvard department and stages no scene in Colombo. That the events motivated the 1986 book is stated in secondary accounts and not independently verified.
stops.campa: In late July mobs move through Colombo carrying electoral registers and burn Tamil houses street by street, and the killing spreads across the island; the dead are counted in the hundreds, the displaced in the tens of thousands. The civil war begins here. He is a Tamil out of Jaffna holding a chair at Harvard, and where he is standing that month no source consulted establishes. Three years later he publishes a book with the word fratricide in the title.
suggested_refs: The anti-Tamil pogrom of July 1983, known as Black July

stops.name: The University of Rochester, the Morgan Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested: the memoir states Lewis Henry Morgan Memorial Lectures, University of Rochester, 1984, which upgrades what earlier passes carried as a reconstruction from series convention. Month not given, defaulted.
stops.campa: At Rochester he gives the Lewis Henry Morgan Memorial Lectures, the series named for the American lawyer who wrote up the Iroquois and made kinship a subject. His own subject is rationality: whether the line drawn between magical thinking and scientific thinking separates two kinds of mind, or two orderings available to the same one. The lectures do not appear as a book until 1990, six years on. In the interval he writes about the war on his own island instead.
suggested_refs: Lewis Henry Morgan Memorial Lectures, University of Rochester, 1984

stops.name: Norton's Woods, Cambridge: the American Academy
stops.date_confidence: election attested to 1984; month arbitrary, set only to order this stop within the year. Coordinates corrected to the Academy's house at 136 Irving Street; a value circulating in earlier passes lands a kilometre and a half north of it.
stops.campa: The American Academy of Arts and Sciences elects him a Fellow. Its house stands at Norton's Woods on Irving Street, a low modern building set back among trees a mile from his office, and the induction is a signature in a book that goes back to 1780. He is fifty-five, and the first Sri Lankan-born anthropologist on its rolls. The National Academy of Sciences in Washington, which carries almost no anthropologists at all, elects him ten years after this one does.
suggested_refs: American Academy of Arts and Sciences, 136 Irving Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts

stops.name: The Peabody Museum, the forest saints and the amulets
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1984; month arbitrary and set only to place the book after the year's two elections. Coordinates are the Peabody Museum on Divinity Avenue, seat of the Harvard anthropology department.
stops.campa: The Buddhist Saints of the Forest and the Cult of Amulets follows Thai monks who leave the monasteries for the forest to meditate alone, and who become, without having asked for it, objects of national veneration. Their images are pressed into amulets. The amulets are worn by soldiers and traded by collectors, catalogued and priced. Charisma turns out to be transferable into small metal objects. Cambridge publishes the book in 1984, and he writes up the market as carefully as he writes up the meditation.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'The Buddhist Saints of the Forest and the Cult of Amulets' (Cambridge UP, 1984)
Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, 11 Divinity Avenue

stops.name: Cambridge, Culture, Thought, and Social Action
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1985, Harvard University Press, 411 pages, per the Internet Archive catalog record. That the 1968 and 1979 pieces are reprinted inside is widely reported but not itemised by that record. That Tambiah is in explicit dialogue with Claude Levi-Strauss is a reconstruction from the volume's subject matter; no source consulted this pass confirms a direct citation. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Harvard University Press collects the essays: four hundred and eleven pages, the Malinowski lecture and the Radcliffe-Brown lecture reworked among them, the galactic polity paper reprinted. Claude Levi-Strauss had read myth and rite as a formal system, a grammar waiting to be solved. This volume argues instead that a rite is a performance, and that its force lies in its being done, in this order, by these people, in front of witnesses who can say afterward that it was done.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Culture, Thought, and Social Action: An Anthropological Perspective' (Harvard UP, 1985)

stops.name: Cambridge, Ethnic Fratricide and the Dismantling of Democracy
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1986. Month defaulted. The place is where the book was written, not a publication event.
stops.campa: Sri Lanka: Ethnic Fratricide and the Dismantling of Democracy. He turns the apparatus built for Thai villages onto his own country and finds there not ancient hatred but recent legislation: a language act, university admissions weighted by ethnicity, a state making its Tamil minority foreign by statute, and the crowds the statutes licensed. He writes as a scholar and as a man whose relatives live there. It is the first of four books he will write on the subject. Nobody bans it.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Sri Lanka: Ethnic Fratricide and the Dismantling of Democracy' (1986)

stops.name: The University of Malaya, Kuala Lumpur
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1987 by the memoir, which names the Fifth Sri Lanka Endowment Fund Lecture and gives no title, month, or text. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: He gives the Fifth Sri Lanka Endowment Fund Lecture at the University of Malaya, in Kuala Lumpur: another plural society across the Bay of Bengal, another arrangement of Malay, Chinese, Indian and Buddhist populations under one flag, one that has done its ethnic arithmetic differently and not without blood either. A Sri Lankan endowment pays for a Sri Lankan to speak in Malaysia about what states do to minorities. The title of the lecture is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Fifth Sri Lanka Endowment Fund Lecture, University of Malaya, 1987

stops.name: Cambridge, the presidency of the Association for Asian Studies
stops.date_confidence: two-stage office, corrected from a bare year: vice-president 1988-89, president 1989-90, with the presidential address published in 1990. The convention city where the address was delivered is NOT established by anything consulted, so the stop stays at his own department rather than staging an unknown hall. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: He is vice-president of the Association for Asian Studies for 1988 and 1989, and its president for the year following. The presidential address is called Reflections on Communal Violence in South Asia and appears in the Journal of Asian Studies in 1990. Which convention hall in which American city he stood in to give it is not established by anything reachable, so the stop stays at his desk on Divinity Avenue, which is where the address was written in any case.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Presidential Address: Reflections on Communal Violence in South Asia,' Journal of Asian Studies 49: 741-760 (1990)

stops.name: Cambridge, Magic, Science, Religion, and the Scope of Rationality
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1990, Cambridge University Press, in the Lewis Henry Morgan Lectures series, six years after the Rochester delivery. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Magic, Science, Religion, and the Scope of Rationality, Cambridge University Press, six years after the Rochester lectures it grew out of. It is the summary of the quarrel he entered in 1968: the discipline's long habit of treating magic as failed science, running from Tylor and Frazer forward, against his own insistence that participation and causality are two orderings of the world available to anybody, the Cambridge don who touches wood on his way out of the lecture room included.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Magic, Science, Religion, and the Scope of Rationality' (Cambridge UP, 1990)

stops.name: University College London, the Daryll Forde Memorial Lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1991 by the memoir; no month, no title recorded. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The Daryll Forde Memorial Lecture at University College London, in Gower Street, named for the Africanist who founded the International African Institute. He is sixty-two. The English discipline that sent him a cheque for an essay in 1964 now sends for him by name, and this is the fourth London lecture the record carries. The memoir enters it as a year and a series title, with nothing said about what he spoke on. Two honorary doctorates arrive in the same twelve months, one from Chicago and one from Peradeniya.
suggested_refs: Daryll Forde Memorial Lecture, University College London, 1991

stops.name: Chicago and Peradeniya, two honorary doctorates in one year
stops.date_confidence: both degrees attested to 1991 by the memoir; months not recorded and the June here is arbitrary. The pin is Chicago; the Peradeniya degree, conferred at 7.2564, 80.5971, is folded into this stop rather than given a scene, since no source establishes that he attended either ceremony.
stops.campa: The University of Chicago, where he taught for three years and left without leaving a story behind, makes him a Doctor of Humane Letters. The University of Peradeniya, where he taught at the beginning, makes him a Doctor of Letters in the same year. Two campuses on opposite sides of the world settle their accounts with him inside twelve months. Whether he stood on either platform, nothing consulted establishes. In Sri Lanka the settlement holds for one more year: the next book he publishes is banned there.
suggested_refs: Honorary Doctor of Humane Letters, University of Chicago, 1991
Honorary Doctor of Letters, University of Peradeniya, 1991

stops.name: Cambridge, Buddhism Betrayed?
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1992, University of Chicago Press, xix + 203 pages with six plates, per the Internet Archive catalog record; the ban in Sri Lanka and the quoted phrase come from the Colombo Telegraph tribute of 3 December 2015. That Tambiah names Olcott and Blavatsky in the book is NOT confirmed by any source consulted and is a reconstruction from its subject matter; their taking of pansil at Kandy in May 1880 is separately attested. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Buddhism Betrayed? Religion, Politics, and Violence in Sri Lanka, University of Chicago Press, two hundred and three pages and six plates. It traces how a religion of renunciation was fitted out as the property of one ethnic majority. The modern phase of that fitting-out opens in 1880, when Henry Steel Olcott and Helena Blavatsky take the Buddhist pansil at Kandy and put Western organizing behind a Sinhalese revival. The line runs from there to monks in politics and monks endorsing war. Colombo bans the book on publication.
stops.quote: the most reviled academic in Buddhist Sinhala society
stops.quote_source: Colombo Telegraph, 'A Buddhist Requiem For Stanley Tambiah,' 3 December 2015, on the reception of the book
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Buddhism Betrayed? Religion, Politics, and Violence in Sri Lanka' (University of Chicago Press, 1992)
The taking of pansil by Olcott and Blavatsky at Kandy, 25 May 1880
sources: Colombo Telegraph, 'A Buddhist Requiem For Stanley Tambiah,' 3 December 2015

stops.name: Kynsey Terrace, Colombo: the Punitham Tiruchelvam Memorial Lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1992 by the memoir, which names the lecture and the venue; the month is arbitrary and set only to place the lecture after the book in the year. Coordinates are the ICES address on Kynsey Terrace, Borella, reconciled to one figure across the sources.
stops.campa: He comes to Colombo, to the International Centre for Ethnic Studies on Kynsey Terrace, and gives the Punitham Tiruchelvam Memorial Lecture in the year his book is banned in the country he is standing in. Part of the fury is the cover: a photograph of the Venerable Maduluwawe Sobhitha with his fist raised, which readers take as an accusation laid against the robe itself. The lecture is named for a woman killed in the same conflict he is describing. He gives it anyway.
suggested_refs: International Centre for Ethnic Studies, Kynsey Terrace, Colombo 8

stops.name: Washington, the National Academy of Sciences
stops.date_confidence: election attested to 1994; the National Research Council's Committee for International Conflict Resolution is attested to 1995, corrected from an undated claim and from the wrong preposition. Both folded into one stop. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The National Academy of Sciences elects him a member, an odd berth for a social anthropologist among the physicists and the biologists on Constitution Avenue. The year after, the National Research Council seats him on its Committee for International Conflict Resolution. The American government's scholarly apparatus is asking the author of two books on communal violence in South Asia whether anything can be done about it. The war on his island is twelve years old. It runs another fourteen.

stops.name: Madison, the Hilldale Lecture and Leveling Crowds
stops.date_confidence: lecture attested to 1996 by the memoir, without month or title; the book is attested to the same year. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: He gives the Hilldale Lecture at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, in the year Leveling Crowds: Ethnonationalist Conflicts and Collective Violence in South Asia appears. The book widens the frame from one island to the subcontinent entire, Karachi and Delhi and Hyderabad and Colombo, and asks what a riot actually is. His answer is that it is not a spasm. It is a form with a repertoire, a set of practised routines a crowd knows how to perform because crowds before it performed them.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Leveling Crowds: Ethnonationalist Conflicts and Collective Violence in South Asia' (1996)

stops.name: Bern, the Balzan acceptance speech
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the Balzan Foundation's own prizewinner page dates the acceptance speech Bern, 18.11.1997. This corrects a Bern/Milan conflation; Milan is the Foundation's administrative seat, not the 1997 ceremony city.
stops.campa: In Bern on the eighteenth of November he accepts the Balzan Prize for Social Anthropology, the first social and cultural anthropologist to receive it. The citation names his analysis of ethnic violence and the dynamics of Buddhist societies. In the speech he sets himself against the fashionable prophecy of a coming clash of civilizations divided along primordial faults of culture, language and religion, a thesis published that same year by a colleague at his own university, and he does it without naming the man.
stops.quote: It would seem that I am the first social and cultural anthropologist to receive this prestigious and generous prize, and I accept it less as an award to me personally and more as a recognition that my discipline has something worthwhile to say about the unity of mankind as well as the variety, richness and problems of its civilizational manifestations.
stops.quote_source: Stanley J. Tambiah, acceptance speech, Bern, 18 November 1997, published by the Fondazione Internazionale Premio Balzan

stops.name: London, the Huxley Memorial Medal
stops.date_confidence: HARD CONFLICT, not resolved. The award is attested to 1997 and the lecture title is recorded, but the Royal Anthropological Institute's tabulated delivery dates put the lecture on 18 November 1997, the same day the Balzan speech was given in Bern. He cannot have been in both cities. One of the two dates is wrong and this pass cannot say which. The month and day here are an arbitrary ordering device only, and no scene is staged on any date.
stops.campa: The Royal Anthropological Institute gives him the Huxley Memorial Medal, its highest honour, thirty-three years after the essay prize, and he delivers the Huxley Memorial Lecture under the title Transnational movements, multiculturalism and ethnonationalism. The subject is what he had come to think mattered more than any clash of blocs: guest workers, immigrants, the forcibly displaced of civil war and ethnic cleansing, and the question of how a plural society is supposed to hold together once they arrive.
stops.quote: There is one other development that beckons increasing attention. It concerns the enormous transnational movements of people for various reasons: in search of employment in the more prosperous industrialized or industrializing countries as guest workers or as immigrants; and as a result of forced displacement of people owing to civil wars and the pogroms of ethnic cleansing and genocide.
stops.quote_source: Stanley J. Tambiah, Balzan acceptance speech, Bern, 18 November 1997, on the same theme as the Huxley Lecture title
suggested_refs: Huxley Memorial Medal and Lecture, Royal Anthropological Institute, 1997

stops.name: Fukuoka, the Academic Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1998; the category is corrected from an undifferentiated 'Fukuoka Asian Culture Prize' to the Academic Prize in anthropology, per the Fukuoka Prize official laureate listing. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: In September the city of Fukuoka gives him the Academic Prize of the ninth Fukuoka Asian Culture Prizes, for anthropology. He uses the occasion to explain his own upbringing at greater length than he had anywhere else: Jaffna, the nine children, the Anglican father who practised law, the mother out of the district chiefs, the school where boys of four communities shared a dormitory through a war. He is sixty-nine. Most of what is known about the Jaffna childhood comes from that talk in Fukuoka.

stops.name: Columbia University, the Mary Keatinge Das Lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1999 by the memoir, which gives the year and the series and nothing further. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The Mary Keatinge Das Lecture at Columbia, up on Morningside Heights, a series named in memory of the American wife of an Indian revolutionary who spent his life being deported between countries. He is seventy. The city he is lecturing in holds one of the transnational populations he has been describing since the Bern speech two years earlier. The memoir gives the year and the series and nothing further. What he said in the hall is not recorded in anything reachable this pass.

stops.name: Carlton House Terrace, the British Academy
stops.date_confidence: election attested to 2000. Coordinates corrected for anachronism: the Academy left Burlington House and had been at 10-11 Carlton House Terrace since 1998, so the 1979 Radcliffe-Brown stop and this one sit at different addresses on purpose. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: The British Academy elects him a Corresponding Fellow. It has moved since he gave the Radcliffe-Brown Lecture at Burlington House twenty-one years earlier, and sits now at Carlton House Terrace above the Mall, two years into the new address. Corresponding fellowship is what the British give a scholar they count as theirs and cannot claim. By 2000 he has been claimed by Ceylon, by Thailand, by England and by America, in that order, and has spent two decades arguing that claims of that kind are the problem. He is seventy-one and has one book left in him.
suggested_refs: The British Academy, 10-11 Carlton House Terrace, London

stops.name: Cambridge, the life of Edmund Leach
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 2002. Month defaulted. That it is his last book is inferred from the bibliographies consulted, which record nothing after it.
stops.campa: Edmund Leach: An Anthropological Life. Thirty-eight years after Leach brought him to Cambridge, and thirteen years after Leach's death, he writes the life of the man who opened the door: the Burma ethnographer, the professional provocateur, the Reith lecturer who told the BBC that the family with its narrow privacy and its tawdry secrets was the source of all our discontents. He is seventy-three. Nothing appears after it, and he lives another twelve years.
suggested_refs: Tambiah, 'Edmund Leach: An Anthropological Life' (Cambridge UP, 2002)

stops.name: 640 Concord Avenue, Cambridge: the Neville Center
stops.date_confidence: attested, and a contradiction resolved rather than left open: the NAS memoir prints 29 January 2014 in both its header and its text, but the Colombo Telegraph tribute published 25 January 2014 reports him dead on the 19th, and an obituary cannot precede its subject's death. The 19th stands; the memoir's date is an error. Coordinates within about 350 metres of the Neville Center.
stops.campa: He dies in Cambridge, Massachusetts on the nineteenth of January, three days past his eighty-fifth birthday, first at his own apartment and then at the Neville Center on Concord Avenue. He is survived by his former wife Mary and by their sons Jonathan and Mathew. The Academy memoir written the year after prints the death as the twenty-ninth, and a tribute out of Colombo dated the twenty-fifth had already reported him six days gone. The nineteenth is the date that can stand.
suggested_refs: Neville Center at Fresh Pond, 640 Concord Avenue, Cambridge, Massachusetts

stops.name: Kynsey Terrace, Colombo: a Buddhist requiem
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Colombo Telegraph report of 3 December 2015. Posthumous stop: the traveller is not present, and it is included as the reception of the work in the hall where he himself lectured in 1992. The reason for the twenty-two month delay is not explained by any source consulted.
stops.campa: Twenty-two months after the death, Colombo holds a public commemoration for him in the auditorium of the International Centre for Ethnic Studies, the hall he lectured in in 1992. Gananath Obeyesekere speaks, and Sarath Amunugama, and John D. Rogers. The city that banned his book on the day it appeared gathers to praise him, and no source explains the delay. Eighteen months earlier the Sunday Times of Sri Lanka had run an editorial headed Buddhism betrayed by extreme monks.
